### Chapter 9: On the nature of Gold.

**S**ome objections must, however, be raised regarding the nature of gold, which, according to Hermes <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure associated with alchemical wisdom</note>, is the only metal in which no "illness" appears. Indeed, neither part of its substance is infected or intemperate. Since it is composed, like other things, of sulfur and quicksilver, its sulfur is most lucid and pure, brought to a state of purity through very powerful washings, possessing absolutely no combustible unctuosity nor any evaporable, phlegmatic watery moisture. It is perhaps sublimated and digested in concave places—where the solid surface is frequently sublimated and digested by a temperate heat, in a process of digestion called *pepansis* <gloss>ripening/maturation</gloss>—and the earthy substance, which is incorporated into the sulfur, is clean and most subtle, suspended in a vaporous state throughout the entire substance of the radical moisture of that sulfur. From this, it follows that the heat of that sulfur is complexional, departing in no way from its temperament; and this acts like the masculine power in the composition of gold.

Likewise, its quicksilver has two substances refined to the extremes. The third element, which is in the heat itself, is subtilized, not merely materially divided, but vaporously refined; it is the most subtle earth, frequently sublimated in the cavities of the earth by the life-giving heat of the sun and the stars. Similarly, the watery element is also subtilized through the same method of repeated subtilization; and since it is thus inwardly subtilized, it is clear that when mixed together through heat and the disposition of the place—which forces and reflects the vapor back upon itself—they are bound with a very strong knot of mixture.

The sulfur does not enter into the composition of gold merely through its quality, but through its substance, and being a subtle substance, it will penetrate everywhere through the quicksilver and, in coagulating, colors it. And since both have been brought by sublimation to the form of the superior elements, which arrive at the nature of transparency with a perpetual body, both will possess the fullness of purity. And when many parts of the matter are thickened, they will exist together; for this is the property of a subtle substance, that when it stands through coagulation, it will have many parts in a very small space. Therefore, the contracted transparency will produce a citrine color, and the subtlety creates maximum consolidation, while the constancy of many parts together in a small place and position creates weight, as is reasonably demonstrated in those things which are shown in the Heavens and the World <note>a reference to Albertus Magnus’s own work, *De Caelo et Mundo*</note>.

From this consolidation and temperament, it follows that gold is little evaporable or not at all, and for this reason, it is almost odorless. Although an odor is not essentially a smoky evaporation, a strong odor is nevertheless frequently associated with smoky evaporation; for this reason, it further follows that gold is more incorruptible than any metal and better withstands fire due to the most powerful intermixture of its components. For a smoky evaporation indicates a certain corruption of bodies, which is less in silver and more in copper. From these things, we have the cause why those things that do not burn gold, such as sulfur, arsenic, and certain others, do burn silver. The cause of this—

<margin>Why gold does not burn.</margin>

<column-break/>

—kind is the mixture, in that all of its earthy portion is in the moisture, defending itself from burning, and all of its moisture is in the earthy portion, restraining itself so that it does not fly away through evaporation, which connection Plato calls *Plo* <note>a corrupted or abbreviated reference to the "binding" or *ploke*</note>, and Empedocles the "glue of the elements." From the temperance of gold, one understands why it is hot and moist, contributing to the trembling of the heart and to melancholy, which makes one sad. Because of this, it helps against those things that make a man speak alone to himself; it helps against the gold-related passions, whether by rubbing the substance of the same virtue or by consuming it ground up. 

Because of its solidity, it does not happen that it touches the bodies it contacts, except with difficulty; and for this reason, it is worn in rings and other ornaments. Silver, however, stains a little, and other metals stain a great deal, which a *continent* <gloss>a containing vessel or substance</gloss> does not touch; this is because the unctuous moisture is entirely separated from them in the whole, to which is commixed the burnt earthy matter in them, and this smears like the soot of an unctuous body. The great purity of the matter causes it to be very rarely found mixed with other bodies, but always as if pure; when it is mixed with others, it cannot retain such purity, and therefore it degenerates into copper. On the contrary, it is very rarely found unless incorporated into stones. And this is again why it is often found as grains of sand, because such purity must necessarily be small and raised from that matter, and as if expelled, and therefore distinct; yet it is already found as a grain of gold mixed with marcasite. 

From these things, it is again clear why these two metals, namely gold and silver, were chosen for the material of coinage by the ancient sages. They possess this special benefit for aiding and comforting the human complexion, and they are more durable and noble than others. The substances that purify gold are sharp and very dry, such as salts, especially sea salts, the soot of unctuous but dry bodies, and ground brick. 

When gold is to be purified, a test vessel is made in the manner of a gourd or a bowl. Above that vessel, one similar to it is made and glued at the place of the contacts with tenacious clay, which alchemists call the *clay of the wise* <note>original: "lutum sapientiae"</note>. In the upper part, there are many holes through which vapor and smoke may exit. Afterward, the gold is thinned into short and thin sheets and arranged in the vessel, so that each layer of sheets, above and below, has a powder of soot, salt, and ground brick mixed together, and it is cooked in a strong fire until it is most pure; and the ignoble substances are consumed within it. The clay of the wise, from which the test vessels are made, is made from ground potsherd, mixed again, and fired. This vessel, when placed in the fire, is not diminished by the sensible consumption of fire. There is, however, another way in which the clay of the wise is prepared in alchemy, but that which goldsmiths use suffices here. 

Thus, therefore, gold is purified, and nothing is burned in it except the ignoble substance, for which reason Hermes elegantly says in his alchemical works: "The sulfur itself, by a certain subtle affinity of sulfur to which all metals are neighbors, burns up all their bodies and reduces them to ash, but gold it does not." ### Chapter Eight: On the nature and admixture of gold.

**S**hould we also object to these points concerning the nature of gold, which alone according to <term>Hermes</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note> is that in which no ailment appears? Neither part of its matter is infected or intemperate. Since, like other things, it is composed of <term>sulfur</term> and <term>quicksilver</term> <gloss>mercury</gloss>, its sulfur is most lucid and most clean, and through most powerful washings, it is brought to a purity that has absolutely no combustible oiliness, nor any aqueous, phlegmatic, evaporable moisture. It is strongly sublimated and digested in concave places whose solid surface often digests it with a temperate heat through a digestion which is called <term>pepansis</term> <gloss>ripening</gloss>. The earthy substance, which is incorporated into the sulfur, is clean and very subtle, suspended vaporously through the whole substance of the radical moisture of that sulfur. From this, it remains that the heat of that sulfur is constitutional, departing in no way from its temperament; and this is like the masculine virtue in the composition of gold. Similarly, its quicksilver has two substances cleansed to the extremes. For the third, which is in the heat itself, is subtilized, not only materially divided, but vaporously, as it is the most subtle earth, often sublimated in the cavities of the earth through the lifegiving heat of the sun and the stars. Similarly, the aqueous part is subtilized through the same manner of iterated subtilization; and when the glass is thus inside, it is subtilized finely. It is evident that once mixed together through heat and the disposition of the place that traps and reflects the vapor upon itself, they are bound by the strongest bond of mixture. Sulfur does not come into the composition of gold only through its quality but through its substance, and since it is a subtle substance, it will penetrate everywhere through the quicksilver and, by coagulating, it colors it. And since both are brought by sublimation to the form of the superior elements which, in the nature of transparency, arrive with a perpetual body, both will have a full purity. And when many parts of the matter are thickened, they will be consistent. This indeed is a property of a subtle substance, that which is consistent through coagulation will have many parts in the smallest space. The transparency, therefore, once contracted, will make a citrine color. And subtlety makes for the greatest solidity, and the consistency of many parts together in a small place and position makes for weight, just as is proven from those things that have been demonstrated reasonably in the <term>Coelum</term> <gloss>Heavens</gloss> and the world. It remains, however, from the solidity and temperament together that gold is little evaporable or not at all; therefore, it is as if it is not odoriferous. An odor, although it is not essentially a smoky evaporation, yet often a strong odor is with a smoky evaporation, because of which it is further concluded that gold is more incorruptible than any metal and more enduring of fire because of its strongest commixture in the mixture. For smoky evaporation indicates a certain corruption of bodies, which is less in silver and more in copper. From these things, we have the cause why those things burn silver that do not burn gold, such as sulfur and arsenic and certain others. The cause of this-

<meta>continues from previous page: ...The centurions told their story, saying they had completed a long journey with the assistance of the King of Ethiopia, through whom they had been granted letters of recommendation to neighboring kings, and thus pushed into the further regions. We arrived, they said, at immense marshes, the end of which neither the inhabitants knew, nor could anyone hope for. The waters and the grasses are so entangled that they are neither navigable by boat, except for a small one capable of holding only one person, nor passable for a foot soldier, as the marsh is muddy and overgrown with weeds. There, they said, we saw two rocks from which a massive force of river water emerged. Whether this is the head of the Nile, or if it is the place where it is born, or if it returns to the earth after having been received from a previous course, I do not know. Do you not believe that, whatever it is, it rises from a great subterranean lake? For it must contain moisture dispersed in several places and collected at the bottom so that it can erupt with such great force. Some judge that earthquakes and fire are not caused by the same thing. This is what he says. He also says: Sometimes a wound occurs where it requires you to perform a complete amputation. As for when a limb—if the surgery requires cutting from it—is not abundant in tissue, it requires flesh-regenerating agents. It is not sufficient to use only what dries and prevents <note>the flow of humors</note>; rather, sometimes the drying and preventing agent, in some respects, disturbs the material from which the growth should occur. The indentation and deficiency in the bone may be such that it cannot fully regenerate, leaving an indentation, similar to a condition that may occur where more than is necessary grows, resulting in proud flesh <note>excessive, unhealthy granulation tissue</note>. The patient who requires flesh regeneration in a wound must avoid anything other than that which is conducive to good growth. The regenerator must be such that it enables the growth of flesh. As for the skin, if it has been completely severed, it does not regenerate in its place; rather, firm flesh grows there upon which hair and veins do not grow. However, branches are generated, and it grows like flesh.

Among the wounds are those of high risk: wounds occurring in the nerves and the muscles of the arm, and we will mention this in the chapter on nerves. Often, unpleasant and severe symptoms follow them. The worst thing that follows a wound to the upper arm is a change in color and a subsequent drop in the pulse, followed by shriveling and coldness, and a collapse of strength. Convulsions may also follow. The same applies to that which occurs in front of the knee at the kneecap, for severe symptoms follow it, and it is a situation from which it rarely escapes. This is what he says. He also says: perhaps the wound occurs in a place where you are obligated to perform a complete amputation. As for the limb, if the wound entails amputation, it does not multiply, but rather requires substances that generate flesh. It is not enough to merely apply drying and preventative agents; in fact, the drying and preventative agent might, in a certain sense, impede the material from which the flesh grows. There may also be a depression and a loss in the bone such that it cannot grow back completely, leaving a cavity. This is a condition that may occur. Sometimes more than necessary grows, resulting in proud flesh <note>original: "لحم زائد" refers to what is medically known as hypergranulation tissue</note>. It is necessary that the patient desiring the growth of flesh in a wound does not use excessive cleansing. The growth agent might be such that it allows the flesh to grow. As for the skin, because if it has been completely severed, flesh grows in its place that is firm and on which hair and veins do not grow, but rather branches originate and it grows like flesh. Among the wounds are wounds of danger: wounds occurring in the nerves and the muscles of the upper arm, and we will mention this in the chapter on nerves, and the bad and severe symptoms that follow them. ### On Lettuce. Chapter XXII.
Lettuce, as Isidore says, is so named from the exuberance of its milky fluid, or because it fills nursing women with milk. In men, it restrains the movement of <term>Venus</term> <gloss>lust/sexual desire</gloss>. Its species is twofold: namely, domestic and wild, which we call <term>feralia</term> <gloss>wild/brutal</gloss>, because its back possesses hard spines like iron, as Isidore says in book seventeen, the last chapter. Regarding this, Pliny says in *On Diets*: wild lettuce is similar in form to domestic lettuce, but it has longer, thinner, rougher, and less green leaves due to the scarcity of its moisture. For this reason, it possesses much bitterness and astringency compared to the domestic kind, because it is of greater heat and dryness. Thus, many say that it provokes menstruation and expels raw humors, as Dioscorides says. Lettuce, in its domestic form, is cold and moist according to the degree, and it does not exceed the limit in either quality. Therefore, its use is for a light medicine, for delicate stomachs, and for the sea <note>referring to the stomach or perhaps a misinterpretation of a source term</note>, which will be fresh. And so it is quickly digested and settles burning and biting of the stomach and red bile; it cools the boiling of the blood and calms insomnia. It cures headache and choleric fumes. It increases milk in women and generates and increases semen in men. This happens because of the goodness of the blood which it generates in perfect quantity and at a perfect age. But when it ages and hardens, its moisture diminishes and it becomes bitter; through its use, very bad blood is generated. The <term>virtus visiva</term> <gloss>visual power</gloss> then fails and is weakened, the cause of which is the mortification of the animal sense, because with its astringency it suffocates the natural spirit. Therefore, such lettuce is most harmful to those wishing to conceive, for the matter congeals and coagulates the seminal fluid, especially if its seed is taken often in food or drink. This is the teaching of Isaac in *On Diets*. However, Pliny says in book twenty, chapter eight, regarding lettuce: there is a species of lettuce born spontaneously which they call <term>caprina</term> <gloss>goat-like</gloss>, which, when placed in the sea, kills fish that are nearby. With its stalk and blunt leaves and sprinkled salt, severed nerves are healed. There is another species of lettuce that grows in fields, whose crushed leaves, applied with porridge, heal ulcers; the Greeks call this <term>ysopon</term> <gloss>hyssop</gloss>. A third species is that which grows in woods, which they call <term>steraton</term>; its crushed leaves heal putrescent wounds, and with the root and leaves, they mitigate <term>ignis sacer</term> <gloss>holy fire/erysipelas</gloss>. There is also another species of this lettuce that is round and short, which many call <term>beratia</term>; its juice, when hawks scratch their eyes, they draw out, and by moistening their eyes with it, they clear away darkness and cloudiness when they age. The juice of this herb heals the eyes of men and is wonderful when human milk is mixed with it. It cures the bites of serpents and the stings of scorpions if its juice is drunk with wine and the crushed leaves are applied as a plaster over the wound. It also disperses and subdues all swelling. The seed of lettuce, both wild and domestic, calms the imaginations of lust in dreams and does not allow the body to be polluted if it is taken frequently in food. However, its frequent and excessive use causes darkness in the eyes. Pliny attributes many other praises to it in the same chapter, but these shall suffice.

He directed Ali ibn Isa ibn Mahan, whom he had released, to Khorasan. When al-Ma'mun heard of this, he dispatched Tahir ibn al-Husayn ibn Mus'ab al-Bushanji from Merv with four thousand men. He met Ali ibn Isa at al-Raqqah and killed him. Then, al-Ma'mun also sent Harthamah ibn A'yan to Iraq. Al-Ma'mun remained in Merv until Muhammad <note>referring to the Caliph al-Amin</note> was killed at the end of Muharram in the year one hundred and ninety-eight, and he was pledged allegiance as Caliph. 

Al-Ma'mun remained in Khorasan in the year one hundred and ninety-nine and in the year two hundred, while sending men to Iraq. He sent Humayd ibn Abd al-Hamid ibn Rib'i al-Ta'i al-Tusi, then he sent Ali ibn Hisham ibn Khusraw al-Marwazi. He then sent the possessor of two honors <note>a title referring to military and administrative leadership</note>, Ali ibn Abi Sa'id ibn Khallad al-Fadl ibn Sahl, over the land tax of Iraq. Then he sent al-Hasan ibn Sahl over all affairs. Harthamah returned from Iraq in anger and went to al-Ma'mun, who imprisoned him. He died in prison three days later in Merv in the year two hundred. 

Then al-Ma'mun pledged allegiance to al-Rida, Ali ibn Musa ibn Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib, in Merv as his heir apparent in the year two hundred and two. He left Merv in that year, traveling at an easy pace, then proceeded to Sarakhs, where he stayed. al-Fadl ibn Sahl, his vizier, was killed in Sarakhs in the bathhouse. Al-Ma'mun executed a group of people because of that event. Al-Ma'mun traveled to Tus; when he arrived in Tus, he stayed there, and this was in the year two hundred and three. Al-Rida died in Tus. Al-Ma'mun had corresponded with all the kings.

Gayatri. Ushnih. Anushtup. Brihati. Pankti. Trishtup. To the Jagati || 1 ||

"Having fashioned the verses into the seven meters, beginning with the Gayatri, in the manner of 'Hail to the Gayatri' <note>original: "gāyatryai svāhā"</note>, and so on according to the meter" (Shāntikalpa 18.1). Since the manner of applying these mantras is shown there in the <term>Shāntikalpa</term> <gloss>Treatise on Rites of Pacification</gloss>, there are seven mantras in this hymn: 'Hail to the Gayatri,' 'Hail to the Ushnih,' 'Hail to the Anushtup,' 'Hail to the Pankti,' 'Hail to the Trishtup,' 'Hail to the Jagati.' All the mantras are clear in their meaning.

The two hymns beginning with 'To the first of the Angirasas' <note>original: "āṅgirasānām ādyaiḥ"</note> are applied in the Great Rite of Pacification <note>original: "mahāśānti"</note> known as the <term>Āṅgirasī</term>, which is prescribed for one who desires to perform a ritual, or for one who is being showered upon by rain, as stated in: "The <term>Āṅgirasī</term> [is] for one who desires a sorceress, and for one who is being rained upon" (Shāntikalpa 17.2). It has been stated in the <term>Shāntikalpa</term>: "The collection" (19.22:23) in the <term>Āṅgirasī</term>. "In the <term>Aindra</term> [rite] beginning with 'Indra, attended by the Maruts' <note>original: "indra marutva"</note> (AV 2.5)" (Shāntikalpa 18.1; 4). Here, the word 'collection' refers to these two hymns.

To the <term>haritas</term>. Hail || 5 ||

To the <term>kshudras</term>. Hail || 6 ||

### CANTO. XXI. OF THE SECOND CANTICLE OF DANTHE.

Noble subject: and nobly treated in this XXI canto. In which he sets forth: how as they followed their path, they were rejoined by a soul: from whom they understood the cause of the shaking of the mountain: and of the singing of the souls. And finally, they recognized this person to have been a poet: whom Virgil recognized with great joy.

<column-break/>

except with the water, for which the young
Samaritan woman asked for grace,
troubled me and haste spurred me
along the encumbered path behind my guide
and I felt sorrow for the just vengeance <note>The suffering of the souls in Purgatory, which is a divine and just retribution.</note>.

THE NATURAL THIRST. He demonstrates that there is an innate thirst and desire in man for knowledge. And because the knowledge of divine things is that through which we are blessed, and we cannot have this perfectly through our own industry, nor by natural means, unless we are illuminated by the Holy Spirit. Which Christ denoted in the Gospel of Saint John, Chapter IV, when asking for a drink from the Samaritan woman at the well of Jacob, and she denying him, alleging that the Jews do not associate with Samaritans, he replied: "If you knew who it is that asks you for a drink, you would ask him, and he would give you a drink of the water from a fountain that springs into eternal life." The young woman then, after many words, asked him, and Christ filled her with the Holy Spirit. Wherefore the poet most wisely demonstrates at present that the natural thirst, that is, the natural desire for knowing and understanding, is never satisfied except with the water, for which the young Samaritan woman asked for grace, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit. TROUBLED ME <note>Italian: "Mitrauagliaua"</note> is a translation from wheat already threshed, which, so that it may remain purified and clean, is "worked," that is, it is made to pass from sieve to sieve; so our soul, wishing to find the truth, purges itself from time to time. AND HASTE SPURRED ME demonstrates that at the same time the soul was eager to investigate the cause of the shaking of the mountain and of the singing of the souls, and the body had to hasten in following its journey. But Statius, appearing, declares that which neither Dante, that is, sensibility, nor Virgil, that is, human intellect—though illuminated by much doctrine—could understand by themselves. But Statius, who is accustomed to such things, declares them. And he sets Statius as the human intellect, which extends itself to comprehend that which cannot be comprehended by way of reason. And by comparison, he demonstrates according to what Luke writes in the 23rd chapter.

The small stems, leaves, flowers, seeds, and seed-pods, preserved in salt, are brought to us in this form and figure that we have described. France now nourishes the shrub. In Cyprus, the caper grows in great abundance. It offers little nourishment to those who eat it, because it excels in the thinness of its parts, being born more for medicine than for food. The fruit is preserved sprinkled with salt, otherwise it quickly feels decay. Fresh, without having experienced salt, it nourishes more than when aged in it, yet it moves the bowels more. When washed and macerated for a while until it puts off all the nature of salt, it does not nourish at all, but invites a languishing appetite. It brings on the menses and elicits phlegm from the head. Seed boiled in vinegar settles toothaches if the mouth is rinsed with it. The dry bark of the root has the same effects. For a level aim from a chariot, the string should be drawn low. Therefore, drawing upward from that position is known as upward aim. <note>verse 48</note>

For a distant target located above, a low aim is used; for a low target, an upward aim; for a level target, a level aim is appropriate. <note>verse 49</note>

A target sixteen fingers in circumference is called a thick target. A subtle target is two fingers in size, with a five-finger crown. <note>verse 50</note>

A target inferred by sound is called a remote or subtle target. Thus, the King should demonstrate these five types of targets in his marksmanship. <note>verse 51</note>

Whether moving sideways, moving forward, rotating, or jumping, their locations are defined in the sky, on the ground, or in the water. <note>verse 52</note>

Two hundred is the excellent distance, one hundred and fifty is the medium distance, and one hundred and twenty is the minor distance, measured in <term>dhanvantara</term> <gloss>bow-lengths</gloss> on the ground. <note>verse 53</note>

The King should strike an excellent distance with four arrows in succession: those with level feathers, those thick and subtle, those without feathers, and those for urban combat. <note>verse 54</note>

He should show his agility by releasing one arrow as it falls, one while in his hand, and five in the sky, and thus the King should strike the target. <note>verse 55</note>

Then, since it pertains to this matter, as was said above, one must see how this reasoning stands. For if one examines it diligently, one will surely find that it is nothing other than a certain order and disposition of things that lead to a proposed end.

In this genre, however, it is customary to consider whether there is some force innate in the things themselves, or whether it depends rather on an external principle. This is indeed the case, such that both often concur. For nature itself has its movements, which reason and art nevertheless perfect and direct.

Wherefore you would not absurdly say that this entire doctrine can be divided into two parts: one of which concerns the knowledge of natural things, and the other in the use and application of the same. The former is indeed called theoretical, while the latter is named practical.

But to return to the matter, one must note especially that which is taught regarding the discipline of soldiers. For not only is strength of spirit required, but also skill with arms and obedience toward leaders. For without these, no army can stand for long, nor can it hope for any victory.

Therefore, the ancients labored with the greatest care to ensure that they had soldiers who were not only robust in body but also prepared in spirit. Hence those most severe laws, hence the daily exercises, by which, once accustomed, they bore every labor easily.

In this chapter, however, which we are now treating, it is shown how all these things are directed toward one goal. For just as in the human body various members perform various duties, so in the republic and in the army various orders are established.

Finally, it must be concluded that all happiness and success depend on a correct foundation. For whoever has laid the foundations well, he will easily build the rest upon them. Conversely, if the principles are corrupt, nothing good is to be expected.
